# Old Light

Step outside on any clear night and look up. It feels immediate — the sky as a ceiling, close and present. But nothing up there is *now*. Every point of light touching your eye left home long ago. The Moon's light is a little over a second old. The Sun's takes eight minutes to arrive, which means if the Sun vanished this instant, we'd go on basking in its glow for eight more minutes, unaware — like someone reading a letter from a friend who died while writing it.

Sirius, the brightest star in our sky, shines down with light eight and a half years stale. Alpha Centauri: over four years. Find the Andromeda Galaxy on a dark night — a faint smudge, the most distant thing visible to the naked eye — and you are receiving photons that departed two and a half million years ago, back when our ancestors were just learning to knap stone. The galaxy you're looking at may not even exist anymore in any form you'd recognize. The image does. Images seem to be permanent.

Astronomers like to say telescopes are time machines, but that makes it sound deliberate. There is no other kind of looking. Distance is depth; the farther you see, the further back. Point an instrument at a quasar and you're reading mail posted billions of years ago by an object that has probably moved on, or ended, or become something else entirely.

We've caught pieces of this mail before. In the year 1054, astronomers in China and Japan recorded a "guest star" — a brilliant intruder bright enough to see in broad daylight for weeks. It was a supernova: a star dying. Its light had crossed roughly six and a half thousand years of emptiness to arrive precisely in time for humans to look up and take notice. Today its remains drift through Taurus as the Crab Nebula, still expanding, still glowing with the energy of that ancient death. Five centuries later, Tycho Brahe watched another "new star" flare and demonstrated it lay far beyond the Moon — proof that the heavens, supposed to be perfect and unchanging, carried corpses. What looked like news was always old news. The newest thing in the sky is the oldest.

And the traffic hasn't stopped. Betelgeuse, the red shoulder of Orion, is due to explode someday — tomorrow, or in a hundred thousand years, or possibly centuries ago, its announcement even now crawling toward us at the fastest speed anything can manage. When it comes, it will briefly rival the Moon, then fade, and astronomers will get to dissect a star that has been dead longer than anyone can say.

Here's the stranger thought: Earth has been broadcasting for about a century. Radio, television, radar — an expanding bubble more than a hundred light-years across, thinning as it spreads but never stopping. The earliest jazz recordings, the first television test patterns, wartime transmissions — all of it is still rolling outward at the speed of light, irretrievable. We cannot call it back. Nothing that ever emitted light or signal gets erased; it only gets far away. The universe doesn't delete. It archives by distance.

You'd think this stops at the edge of the atmosphere, but it doesn't. The same law runs the room you're sitting in. Light crosses about a foot per nanosecond, so the face of a friend across the table reaches you a few billionths of a second after it left them. Everyone you have ever seen, you saw slightly in the past. Every conversation is a duet performed with echoes. The delays are too small to matter, but the principle is absolute: perception is always retrospective. By the time you register anything at all, it is already history.

Which is, I think, why memory behaves the way it does. The people we've lost keep arriving in us like old light — a phrase, a way of laughing, the specific weight of their silence — signals launched long ago from sources that have gone dark. Grief is the discovery that the transmission continues after the transmitter is gone. But there's a comfort folded into the same physics: nothing truly witnessed is ever destroyed. It radiates outward. It becomes part of the permanent record of things, written in a medium that does not decay, only disperses.

So look carefully. At the sky, certainly, but also at the kitchen table, the street at dusk, the faces across from you. Everything you attend to is already leaving at the speed of light, and attention is the only way to keep any of it — not by holding on, since nothing can be held, but by receiving each arrival completely while it lands. The universe keeps an archive, but it only writes down what somebody bothers to notice.

Be somebody who notices.

- Time and perception
- Language itself

I think an essay that blends personal-feeling reflection with interesting ideas would work well. Let me consider a few angles:

Option A: An essay about the deep sea — the fact that most of our planet's habitable space is underwater, dark, unexplored. There's something poetic about that.

Option B: An essay about silence — how rare true silence is, what it means, the sound of a room when nothing happens.

Option C: An essay about maps — how every map is a lie, a compression, and yet we trust them with our lives.

Option D: A short story — maybe something quiet and strange. A lighthouse keeper who receives letters addressed to the light itself. Or a story about someone who inherits a house full of clocks.

Let me think about which would be most engaging and well-crafted. The blue essay has been done a lot (there's a famous Radiolab episode, Rebecca Solnit's book). The deep sea is also well-trodden but still fascinating.

What about writing about something more unexpected? Like:
- The history of the semicolon
- Why old photographs show people not smiling
- The concept of "sonder" (though that's a neologism)
- Liminal spaces
- The way cities smell at different hours
